title: Broadcast-head gain and fidelity
takeaway: For the J-lens vectors, the top 1% of workspace-layer attention heads both amplify those directions strongly and copy them without scrambling, and they separate cleanly from the best heads found for every control population. The paper reads this as weight-level evidence that a small set of heads is specialized for relaying J-space content between token positions.
walkthrough:
This figure reports a search for [[attention-head]]s that specialize in moving [[j-space]] content from one token position to another. The previous subsection showed that MLP blocks amplify J-space directions across depth, measured by [[mlp-gain]]. This figure covers the transformer's other axis: attention, which carries information across the sequence.

Both metrics here are computed from weights alone, with no forward passes. Every attention head has an [[ov-circuit]], the matrix $W_{OV}$ describing what the head writes about whatever it attends to. For a population $P$ of unit directions, a head's gain is the mean of $\|W_{OV}\,v\|$ over $v \in P$, normalized by the same head's gain on isotropic random directions, so that a value of 1 means no preference. [[label-preservation]] asks whether the head copies directions faithfully rather than mixing them up: for each $v_i$, the cosine $\cos(W_{OV}\,v_i, v_i)$ is ranked among the cosines of $W_{OV}\,v_i$ with every other $v_j$, and the mean reciprocal rank is reported against the same statistic on random directions, so a head that copies everything indiscriminately scores zero. A head scoring high on both selectively relays $P$.

For each population, heads are ranked by each metric separately, scored by their worse rank, and the best 1% of workspace-layer heads are kept as that population's [[broadcast-heads]]. Each population therefore gets its own best-case head set; the figure asks whether any population's best heads are actually distinctive.

Six populations appear: the [[j-lens-vector]]s; the same vectors under a fixed random orthogonal rotation, which keeps their spectrum and pairwise geometry but breaks their alignment with the model; [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions in three strata by [[lens-kurtosis]] (top 1%, top 5%, and the middle 25–75%); and MLP output-weight rows. Each marker is the median over that population's broadcast heads, and each bar spans the interquartile range, on both metrics.

The J-aligned populations — J-space, SAE top 1%, SAE top 5% — sit well above the non-J-aligned controls on both axes, and among the SAE strata the highest-κ one scores highest. The rotated control matters most: geometry alone does not earn broadcast heads. The paper takes this as evidence, stated as a suggestion, that a head subset selectively broadcasts J-space content, and notes that these heads concentrate in the first half of the [[workspace-layers]].

terms.definition: For a given population of directions, the top 1% of workspace-layer attention heads after ranking on gain and label preservation separately and scoring each head by its worse rank. The paper's name for the heads that selectively relay that population between token positions.

How strongly a head's OV circuit amplifies a population: the mean of $\|W_{OV}\,v\|$ over the population's unit directions, normalized by the same head's response to isotropic random directions, so 1 means no preference.

Whether a head copies directions faithfully rather than scrambling them among one another: the mean reciprocal rank of $\cos(W_{OV}\,v_i, v_i)$ among the cosines with all other population members, contrasted with random directions so an indiscriminate copier scores zero.
The combined value-then-output transformation of an attention head: what the head writes into the residual stream about the content it attends to, independent of where it attends.
A set of unit directions in residual-stream space whose broadcast is being measured; six populations are compared, each getting its own top-1% head set.

The population of J-lens vectors — one direction per vocabulary token per layer, encoding the model's potential to verbalize that token. The population the paper claims has genuinely distinctive broadcast heads.

The same J-lens vectors under a fixed random orthogonal rotation, which preserves their spectrum and pairwise geometry but destroys their alignment with the model's weights. A control ruling out geometry alone as the explanation.
Sparse-autoencoder decoder directions in the top 1% by J-lens kurtosis κ — the stratum most strongly aligned with the J-space. Its broadcast heads score highest among the SAE strata on both metrics.
The SAE decoder-direction stratum in the top 5% by J-lens kurtosis; also counted among the J-aligned populations that are strongly broadcast.
The middle stratum of SAE decoder directions by J-lens kurtosis — features with weak J-space alignment. A non-J-aligned control whose best heads score low.
The output-weight rows of MLP neurons — the directions individual neurons write into the residual stream. A non-J-aligned control population.
The statistic used to stratify SAE features: how sharply peaked a direction's J-lens vocabulary readout is, taken as a measure of how strongly the direction lies in the J-space.
The reciprocal of the correct item's rank, averaged over the population; here it scores how often $W_{OV}\,v_i$ stays closest to its own $v_i$ rather than to some other member.
Each population's plotted point is the median value of the metric over that population's broadcast heads.
Each bar spans the 25th to 75th percentile of the metric over that population's broadcast heads, showing spread rather than uncertainty of the median.
The middle band of the model's depth where the J-space carries meaningful content; only heads in this range are candidates for broadcast heads, and the J-space's heads concentrate in its first half.

numbers.meaning: The fraction of workspace-layer attention heads kept as a population's broadcast heads, after scoring each head by its worse rank across the two metrics. A deliberately small cut, matching the claim that relaying is the job of a few specialized heads rather than of attention generally.

The number of populations compared: J-lens vectors, their random rotation, three SAE κ-strata (top 1%, top 5%, 25–75%), and MLP output-weight rows. Chosen so that the J-space is tested against controls matched on geometry (rotation), on method (SAE strata), and on being real model weights (MLP outputs).

The κ-percentile boundaries of the two other SAE strata shown. The top strata are J-space-aligned by construction; the 25–75% middle band serves as the weakly aligned control, and the ordering of their scores tracks κ.
The gain of an isotropic random direction, by normalization. Any population median near 1 means the heads treat that content no differently from noise.

The label-preservation score of a head that copies all directions indiscriminately, because the metric is contrasted against the same statistic on random directions. Positive scores therefore indicate selective, faithful copying.
